en: The Sūtra on Discernment, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the early morning.
Having adjusted his robes in the morning, he sat with solemn dignity.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Inform the bhikṣus that they should all listen in silence and clarity; I shall now speak to you of the suffering experienced by human beings."
Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, and said to the Buddha:
“I wish and desire to hear [the teaching].
The Buddha said:
“People have six evils by which they injure and deceive themselves.
What are these six? The eye is deceived by forms;

the ear is deceived by sounds; the nose is deceived by fragrances; the mouth is deceived by flavors; the body is deceived by tactile sensations; and the mind falls into wrong thoughts and is thus deceived by those wrong thoughts.”
"These are the six deceptions that cause people to fall into the evil realms from which there is no time of escape; only the wise truly awaken to this!
The Buddha said:
"From three things, a person may obtain three kinds of suffering."
What are the three types of actions that may be performed?
First, bodily actions that may consist of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct;
second, verbal actions that may consist of double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, lying, or frivolous chatter.
Third, the mind may be subject to greed, anger, and delusion.
Because of these three susceptibilities, one falls into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
These constitute the three types of suffering, which only the wise perceive.
The Buddha said:
"A person has six indulgences that lead to falling into eighteen sufferings.
What are the six indulgences?

The eye indulges in forms; the ear indulges in sounds; the nose indulges in fragrances; the mouth indulges in flavors; the body indulges in tactile sensations; and the mind indulges in perverse thoughts.
These are the six indulgences; they are also called "receptions" and "declines. Because of them, one falls into the eighteen hells, where suffering is long-lasting and there is no time of escape.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a person serves the Buddha and receives the precepts, can they attain liberation from this suffering?
The Buddha said:

“There are those who serve the Buddha and receive the precepts, attaining immeasurable merit that cannot be compared by analogy; yet there are also those who serve the Buddha and fall into extreme transgressions.
Ānanda asked the Buddha, “One who serves the Buddha and receives the Buddha’s precepts should obtain merit; why then would they further incur deep transgression? What is the reason for this?”
"I wish to hear its meaning.
The Buddha said:

"If there is a person who serves the Buddha, upholds the sutras and precepts, and practices with diligence without transgression, they shall obtain immeasurable merit that cannot be illustrated by analogy."
The Buddha said:

"There are those who serve the Buddha and receive the precepts but do not uphold them; they are unable to practice diligence, meditative concentration, or contemplation. They merely rely on the name of serving the Buddha while exclusively engaging in perverse deeds, greedily seeking more without satiety and lacking knowledge of contentment.

They indulge in lustful desires, take pleasure in singing and dancing, and are addicted to the taste of wine, allowing themselves to run wild. Though they claim to serve the Buddha, their transgressions are immeasurable."
For this reason, they shall long fall into the three miserable realms, enduring myriad forms of suffering, from which it is difficult to escape.
The Buddha said:
"There are three grades of those who serve the Buddha: [text continues]"
The first group serves the Buddha as disciples of Māra;
the second group serves the Buddha for the sake of gods and humans;
the third group serves the Buddha as true disciples of the Buddha.
"What is meant by a disciple of Māra serving the Buddha? The Buddha said:

"Though they receive the Buddha’s precepts, their hearts delight in heterodox practices—such as divining omens, exorcising spirits, and performing sacrifices; they place their faith in household elders and patrons rather than in the True and Righteous; they do not know that there are karmic retributions for evil deeds; they merely use the name of 'serving the Buddha' as a pretext while constantly associating with the heterodox. Upon death, they fall into the Avīci Hell, where they suffer for a long time."
After a long time they emerge, yet they remain subjects of the realm of Māra; being sycophantic, flattering, and deceitful, they are difficult to deliver.

Such people as these, through the remaining merit of their past lives, may briefly encounter the Right Path for a moment; however, their minds are clouded and dull, making it difficult for them to understand what they have already received. Consequently, they shall once again enter into endless false views.
"This is what it means for a disciple of Māra to serve the Buddha.
"What is meant by humans and devas serving the Buddha?
"It is to receive and uphold the five precepts, practice the ten wholesome deeds, and never violate them even unto death."
"Believing in the existence of sin and merit—that by doing this one obtains that—and being reborn in the heavens after the end of one's life;
this is what it means for humans to serve the Buddha.
What is meant by a disciple of the Buddha serving the Buddha?"

“Uphold the right precepts, study the sutras and precepts extensively, and cultivate supreme wisdom. Knowing the suffering of the three realms, do not take pleasure in or become attached to them; desiring liberation, practice the four immeasurables and the six perfections.
Take pity on sentient beings and desire to bring them peace and salvation;
do not covet body or life, know that death leads to birth, seek long-term increase in merit, and do not perform evil deeds.”
"This is what it means for a disciple of the Buddha to serve the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"A thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, the path of Māra shall flourish; the age will be one of great evil, with no constant ruler in the land and no permanent dwellings for the people."
When people from distant lands enter the Middle Kingdom, they will plunder, kill, and act with such cruelty that no law or order remains.
At such a time, the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-dharma) shall flourish.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by 'semblance-dharma' (pratirūpa-dharma)?
The Buddha said:
"In the future, bhikṣus will not uphold the True Dharma; they will take wives and raise children, lacking any sense of shame or remorse.
They will treat plowing fields and planting crops as their regular occupation, no longer engaging in study, meditation, or spiritual practice.
They will delight in worldly customs, regarding them as elegant and refined; they will gaze at one another with feigned composure, all following suit from the highest to the lowest."
They cast aside the fundamental basis for crossing over the world through mutual instruction, becoming deluded by form and desire, and showing no fear of sin.
At that time, there were those who knew the Dharma and spoke true mantras to teach and reveal the True Dharma; yet [the former] conceived hatred and jealousy, wishing to destroy them.
They establish polemical arguments, selectively seizing upon both the long and the short, slandering and driving others away until they are left despondent.
For this reason, the Great Dharma gradually diminishes.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"At that time, were there any who honored the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
“There are many who serve the Buddha and have even left the household life, yet they do not uphold the precepts and harbor mutual jealousy;
those who understand the meaning are few, while most lack comprehension.”
Ānanda said:
"At that time, which country will be the most wicked, with people who do not believe in or practice the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"In the land of China there shall be a thousand bhikṣus together in a great kingdom, fallen within the realm of Māra.
Among them, only one or two who are wise shall be true disciples of the Buddha."
"Those born among the six classes of celestial beings are likewise few and far between;
those dwelling in the realm of Māra are exceedingly many, exceedingly many.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

"After my parinirvāṇa, there will likewise be many followers of external paths who come seeking my Way. Those who wish to be ordained should be examined and scrutinized for three months; once it is known that their resolve is capable of practicing pure conduct—that they are empty and tranquil, have few desires, and do not engage in defiled behavior—they may then be accepted."

First, they are taught the ten wholesome actions; after three years have passed, having cultivated the aspiration for the Way and refrained from committing evil deeds, they then receive the two hundred and forty precepts.

In performing the matters of dignified conduct, they diligently maintain their practice, all tending toward liberation; this is what Maitreya ought to establish, from which they shall attain deliverance, thereby corresponding to the Way.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
“As the Buddha has taught, I shall receive it all upon the crown of my head and proclaim it to future generations, so that the Buddha’s propagation of the Dharma shall not be severed.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda, “All that you have received before and after [this teaching] has been integrated into your heart; I also know that you possess faith and protection toward the Buddha-dharma.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:

"Suppose that in the future there is someone who believes in and delights in the Dharma, who seeks it with a sincere heart, and who would sever worldly ties and depart from secular ways to follow the Right Path.

If at that time there were no master to transmit the teachings and precepts, but there were instead one person who transcribed the Vinaya and bestowed it upon him, would he be able to attain deliverance and become a follower of the Way?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"All shall indeed receive it.
Only when one understands the prohibitive Dharma can the precepts be conferred; it is not the case that merely receiving them through written words constitutes being in accordance with the Dharma."

Why is this? The Buddha is the one of supreme wisdom in the heavens above and the world below, the one of supreme magnanimity in the heavens above and the world below, and the one of supreme illumination in the heavens above and the world below. His teachings must not be transmitted recklessly so as to lose their essential meaning; rather, all who receive them must clearly understand the precepts, laws, and prohibitions, becoming thoroughly proficient in every detail before they may pass them on.

To fail to understand the essential matters of the Dharma and its precepts, yet recklessly bestow the methods of ordination upon others, thereby violating the Buddha’s sincere trust and instead regarding such actions as correct—this is a grave offense, no small matter.
"It is fitting that you examine this with discernment.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the future final age, if there are those who, with utmost sincerity and intent, grow weary of suffering and desire to seek liberation, yet no Buddha exists in the world, by what means shall their aspiration for deliverance be fulfilled?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"You should take him to those who clearly understand the Dharma of the precepts and are well-versed in the essential matters of majestic deportment and prohibitions; such a person should be delivered, and upon being delivered, he shall attain deliverance."
"Being ignorant oneself and yet further instructing others, both lose their way; becoming utterly chaotic and without end, from where could they possibly attain deliverance?

The Buddha said, "In the future, there will be bhikṣus who cannot purify themselves, who keep wives and raise children, whose conduct is defiled, who greedily seek offerings, and who do not believe in sin and merit while hoping for peace and happiness. It will be difficult for them to escape, which is truly pitiable."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“In such a future age, those who don the robes of the Way shall all do so through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; by means of this, those people will attain the causes and conditions for perfect truth and shall thereby achieve liberation.”
"For what reason do they again lack faith and contravene the Buddha’s clear teachings? Will they not have to undergo suffering and pain for yet more incalculable kalpas?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"All of these, throughout incalculable kalpas of their previous lives, fell into long-lasting suffering. While in that state of pain, they themselves repented and reproached themselves, vowing to perform good deeds so that they might be liberated from it."
By virtue of the merit from a single moment of self-reproach, he immediately obtained blessings;
consequently, he was born in the final age of the Dharma, where he was able to briefly behold the Buddhist scriptures and further shave his hair to become a bhikṣu.

Because the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) has not yet been fettered, the mind and its mental factors remain hesitant; being dim and lacking clarity, there is defilement, such that for the most part one cannot leave the mundane world and does not encounter bright wisdom.
"In this way, in the future, you shall again fall into extreme suffering and undergo the retribution for your offenses for incalculable kalpas.
The Buddha said, "O bhikṣus!"

Since you have left the household life, abandoned your wife and children, renounced worldly conduct, and become a śramaṇa, you should cultivate the practice of the precepts according to the Dharma of an Arhat. It would be better to pour molten copper into your mouth, which would pass through and burn your stomach and intestines, than to consume the faithful offerings of others without virtue;
it would be better to have your hands cut off with a sharp knife or to have your body dismembered, than to receive the faithful offerings of others without virtue.

If a person lacks the power of virtue yet accepts the faithful offerings of others, they shall fall into the suffering of sin for many kalpas; only after a long time do they emerge, and by means of the remaining trifling merit, they obtain a human body. They must then once again repay each debt individually—some repaying by becoming slaves, some repaying by becoming children, and some repaying by becoming parents.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by 'repaying a debt'?
The Buddha said:
"There are those who serve as slaves and servants whom their masters beat and strike without reason; yet these slaves accept it without harboring resentment.
They labor diligently at their tasks, undaunted by toil and fatigue;
they cherish the property of their masters, not daring to let it go to waste."
This is what it means to be a slave repaying debts in the present life.

Having received the offerings of the faithful from previous lives and failed to practice meritorious deeds, one comes to repay those offenses once the karmic retribution is exhausted; yet because the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) still persists, there is no resentment, but only a willing acceptance.
"What is meant by a son who repays his debts?
It is when the son acquires wealth, yet the parents spend it without restraint, and the son’s heart likewise feels no sense of regret; this is called a son who repays his debts."
"What is meant by 'repaying one's debts to one's parents'?

When parents provide wealth, the children take charge of its expenditure; the parents do not cherish it for themselves, allowing them to obtain whatever they require. All of this is a repayment based on the causal conditions of past consciousness, and therefore there is no sense of stinginess."
All such repayments of debts arise from the convergence of causes and conditions; once the confrontation is concluded, they disperse again, and nothing remains permanent.
The wise realize this and therefore do not engage in them.
Only through virtue and morality can one preserve [this state] for long.

In my previous lives, I have also repaid debts on behalf of slaves, children, and parents; such instances are beyond counting, for all are subject to the conditions of the moment and are difficult to escape.
Having attained the Way up to this day, I see that my parents were all karmic conditions for my virtue and wisdom in previous lives; it was not a matter of repaying a debt.

Throughout successive lifetimes, my parents relinquished me so that I might study the Way; through diligent effort across many kalpas, I have now succeeded in becoming a Buddha—all of this is due to the kindness of my parents.
Those who wish to study the Way must be diligent and filial; otherwise, they will fall into two types of ruin and lose their human seed, not regaining it for kalpas on end.
In this age of the five degenerations, one should maintain proper conduct and follow the teachings; having encountered the Way of the Sūtras, one must not fail to be diligent.
Having encountered the era of a Buddha, one must not fail to receive the teachings with earnest attention and fix them within the heart.
Having encountered an enlightened person, one must not fail to diligently inquire of them and respectfully receive their teachings.

Why is this? Because a human body is difficult to obtain; the six sense faculties are difficult to possess in full; talent and intelligence are difficult to acquire; a Buddha is difficult to meet; and the sutras are difficult to hear. Therefore, one ought to be diligent.
The Buddha said:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there shall come an age of the five heinous crimes. At that time, in the land of China, demonic activities shall flourish and obstruct the Right Path."
Although there are sutras and teachings, those who study them are few;
and even among those who study them, those who practice them are few.

Among the bhikṣus in the world, few are able to maintain pure conduct for themselves; most engage in defiled practices that conform to worldly customs, walking with lofty mien and bearing themselves as if they were no different from ordinary people.
They seek fine clothing, study worldly rhetoric, and pursue worldly ceremonies and expenditures; they follow along with their factions to gratify their own minds and seek worldly fame.
They teach others to enter the Dharma and ordain them as disciples, yet they do not teach them to protect against Māra nor rely upon the True Path.
Regarding the practice of transcending the world, they neither study nor inquire after wisdom.
Claiming one’s own virtue to be great, one fails to guard the gates of the senses;

though having attained human form, it is but a temporary state, yet one considers it eternal. Failing to recognize the great adversary, one shall thereafter undergo suffering that knows no end. To be thus inverted and overturned, falling among the hosts of Māra—how painful this is!
"O Bhikṣus!

Having already obtained a human body and with the six sense faculties fully intact, you behold the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts; you should diligently practice what ought to be practiced and recite them.
Once the foundation of humanity is lost, it is difficult for it to be regained again."
"A Buddha appears in the world but is difficult to encounter; the sutras and the Dharma are difficult to hear. You should each reflect upon this.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, all the bhikṣus sat with solemn composure; through their own reflection, they immediately attained arhatship.
The Sūtra on Discernment Spoken by the Buddha
